notes.meaning: Elijah proposes a public test where each side will pray to their god, and whichever god sends down fire is the true God. The people agree at once because the test sounds completely fair. Since the Canaanites claimed Baal controlled weather and lightning, this challenge met their false god on his own ground.

Elijah tells the hundreds of Baal prophets to choose their bull and begin first because they are so numerous. He makes sure they do not light any fire of their own beneath the wood. Giving them the first opportunity ensured that their total failure would be clear to everyone.

The false prophets dress the bull and shout to Baal from morning until midday, begging him to answer. They leap and perform an agitated ritual dance around the altar they made. In spite of all their desperate cries, the sky remains completely silent.

At noon, Elijah begins mocking them, telling them to shout louder since Baal might be busy, traveling, or asleep. Heathen worshippers often thought their gods had human weaknesses and needed waking up. Elijah uses sharp sarcasm to expose how foolish it is to worship an imaginary god.

The prophets scream even louder and slash their bodies with knives and spears until blood pours over them. Following their pagan customs, they believed shed blood and self-inflicted pain would force their god to show pity. False religion often drives people to harmful extremes in search of answers.

The afternoon wears on as the prophets continue their frantic raving until the time of the regular evening offering. There is still no voice, no answer, and no sign that anyone is listening. Sincere devotion to an idol always ends in complete silence and disappointment.

Elijah calls all the onlookers to gather close so they can examine every single detail. He then rebuilds the altar of the Lord on Mount Carmel, which had been torn down and abandoned. True worship must be restored before God will display His power.

Elijah selects twelve stones, representing the twelve tribes descended from Jacob, whom God named Israel. Although the nation had split into two separate political kingdoms, they were still one family bound to the Lord by His covenant promise. This showed that God still claimed all twelve tribes as His own.

With these stones, Elijah builds an altar dedicated to the name of the Lord. He digs a wide trench around the base large enough to hold about two measures of grain seed. This prepared the site for an undeniable demonstration of God's mighty power.

Elijah carefully arranges the firewood, cuts the bull into pieces, and lays it on the altar according to God's law. Then he orders the people to pour four large jars of water over the meat and the wood. Soaking the sacrifice proved beyond doubt that no hidden coals were buried beneath the altar.

Elijah commands the helpers to pour four more jars of water a second time and then a third time. In all, twelve jars are poured out, completely drenching the offering and the wood. This bold order showed that Elijah was fully confident God could ignite a thoroughly soaked sacrifice.

The water pours down all sides of the altar and fills the surrounding ditch to the brim. Under ordinary conditions, lighting wet wood would be impossible. The soaked ground removed any suspicion of human trickery when the fire arrived.

At the hour of the regular evening offering, Elijah steps forward and prays to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. He asks the Lord to prove publicly that He is the only God in Israel and that Elijah has acted on divine orders. Elijah rested his prayer entirely on God's ancient covenant promises.

Elijah begs the Lord to answer his prayer so the crowd will realize that the Lord is God. He asks God to turn their straying hearts back to Himself. His central desire was God's honor and the spiritual recovery of the nation.

Supernatural fire falls instantly from heaven and consumes the meat, the wood, the stones, the soil, and even the water in the trench. The absolute destruction of the wet materials left no doubt that the Lord had intervened. God proved that He alone governs the forces of nature.

When the crowd witnesses the falling fire, they throw themselves facedown on the earth in deep reverence and awe. They shout together that the Lord alone is God, completely renouncing Baal. Seeing God's undeniable power led the people to humble themselves in worship.

Elijah orders the crowd to capture all the prophets of Baal without letting a single one escape. They bring the false prophets down to the Kishon Valley and execute them in accordance with God's law in Deuteronomy, which condemned those who led Israel into idolatry. Ahab offers no resistance because the verdict from heaven was clear.

Elijah tells King Ahab to go up, eat, and drink because a heavy rainstorm is approaching. Even though the sky was completely dry, Elijah heard the promise of rain by faith. The long drought could now end because the people had turned back to the Lord.

Ahab goes off to eat, while Elijah climbs to the crest of Mount Carmel to pray. The prophet bends low to the ground and buries his face between his knees in deep humility and concentration. This posture expressed his urgent, heartfelt supplication to God for the promised rain.

Elijah directs his servant to walk up higher and look toward the Mediterranean Sea for weather signs. The servant returns saying he sees nothing, but Elijah patiently tells him to go back seven times. True faith persists in prayer even when there is no quick sign of an answer.

On the seventh look, the servant reports a tiny cloud rising from the sea no larger than a man's hand. Elijah immediately recognizes God's answer and warns Ahab to hitch up his chariot before the heavy mud blocks his path. God frequently brings great blessings out of very small beginnings.

The sky quickly turns black with swirling winds and heavy clouds, unleashing a massive downpour on the dry land. Ahab drives his chariot through the storm toward his royal residence in Jezreel. God faithfully kept His promise to end the drought after years of famine.

The Lord grants Elijah supernatural energy, enabling him to tuck his outer robe into his belt and run on foot ahead of Ahab's horses. He runs about seventeen miles through the storm to the entrance of Jezreel. By running before the king, Elijah showed humble respect for the ruler while celebrating the Lord's great victory.
